etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From earlier clowne, cloyne (“man of rustic or coarse manners, boor, peasant”). likely of North Germanic origin, akin to Icelandic klunni (“clumsy fellow, klutz”), Swedish kluns (“clumsy fellow”), all from Middle Low German klunz, from klunt (“pile, lump, something thick”); according to Pokorny, this could be related to a group of Germanic derivatives of Proto-Indo-European *gel- (“to ball up; amass”), such as Proto-West Germanic *klott (“lump”), Proto-Germanic *klūtaz (“clod, lump”), *kultaz (“lump, bundle”), etc.

Alternatively, directly from Low German (compare North Frisian klönne (“clumsy fellow, klutz”), Dutch kluns (“clumsy fellow, klutz”), Dutch kloen (“uncouth person, lout”)), themselves from the same ultimate source as above.

Unlikely from Latin colōnus (“colonist, farmer”), although learned awareness of this term may have influenced semantic development.

definitions.definition: A slapstick performance artist often associated with a circus and usually characterized by bright, oversized clothing, a red nose, face paint, and a brightly colored wig.

quote.citation: 2008, Lich King, “Black Metal Sucks”, in Toxic Zombie Onslaught:
quote.text: Over there in Norway, the churches all burn down / Let's go dress in goth clothes and get painted like a clown

definitions.definition: A person who acts in a silly fashion.

quote.citation: 2013, Kim Stanley Robinson, The Gold Coast: Three Californias (Wild Shore Triptych; 2)‎[1], Tom Doherty Associates, →ISBN, page 122:
quote.text: Everything’s on the table, the specs are there in the RFP and can’t be changed by some clown in the Air Force who happens to come up with a new idea.

quote.citation: 2017, Arron Crascall, See Ya Later: The World According to Arron Crascall:
quote.text: 'Breaking my sister's heart then getting pissed with his mates in the very next pub while she's sobbing alone?' I dragged this clown away from the fruitie and back to Amy next door, running my mouth off at him as we went.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) A man of coarse nature and manners; an awkward fellow; an illbred person; a boor.

quote.citation: a. 1587, Philippe Sidnei [i.e., Philip Sidney], “(please specify the folio)”, in [Fulke Greville; Matthew Gwinne; John Florio], editors, The Countesse of Pembrokes Arcadia [The New Arcadia], London:  […]  [John Windet] for William Ponsonbie, published 1590, →OCLC:
quote.text: This loutish clown is such that you never saw so ill - favoured a vizar
[…]  three things ought always to be kept under: a mastiff dog, a stone horse and a clown; and really I think a snarling, cross-grained clown to be the most unlucky beast of three.

definitions.definition: (obsolete) One who works upon the soil; a rustic; a churl; a yokel.

quote.citation: 1782–1785, William Cowper, “(please specify the page)”, in The Task, a Poem, […], London:  […]  J[oseph] Johnson;  […], →OCLC:
quote.text: The clown, the child of nature, without guile.

quote.citation: August 25, 1759, Samuel Johnson, The Idler No. 71
quote.text: He  […]  began to descend to familiar questions, endeavouring to accommodate his discourse to the grossness of rustic understandings. The clowns soon found that he did not know wheat from rye, and began to despise him; one of the boys, by pretending to show him a bird's nest, decoyed him into a ditch;  […]

quote.citation: 2006, Tropical Fish Hobbyist, volume 54, numbers 5-8, page 32:
quote.text: While the tomato clownfish Amphiprion frenatus has been spawned in captivity, wild-caught tomato clowns are more often seen for sale.

definitions.definition: (intransitive) To act in a silly or playful fashion.

quote.citation: 2006, Noire [pseudonym], Thug-A-Licious: An Urban Erotic Tale, New York, N.Y.: One World, Ballantine Books, →ISBN, page 128:
quote.text: Except for Rasheena, the rest of the baby mamas was at least struggling to live halfway right. They used to clown and act shitty whenever they came by Noojie's and saw Carmiesha there. But every last one of them ended up being grateful to her for the things she did for their kids.

definitions.definition: (transitive, African-American Vernacular) To ridicule, make fun of.

quote.text: The show Dismissed was one of my favorites, because I like to see people get clowned.
All my comrades were laughing and clowning me, but shit, that didn't stop me from talking more shit.
